title: “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth occur?” “Venerable sir, when beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, delighting here and there, thus future…
content: “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth occur?” “Venerable sir, when beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, delighting here and there, thus future rebirth occurs.” “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth not occur?” “Venerable sir, when ignorance is abandoned, knowledge arises, and craving is destroyed, thus future rebirth does not occur.”

title: Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches, And all phenomena — Desirable, delightful, agreeable — Thus they are called. Devas and humans in the world, Regarding them…
content:
Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

For the good person with open eyes,
Light is clearly seen —
Living close, they know clearly,
Skilled in the great Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.

title: “Monk, when a person dwells with sense faculties unguarded, without moderation in eating, not committed to wakefulness, not watching over wholesome states, not devoted to…
content: “Monk, when a person dwells with sense faculties unguarded, without moderation in eating, not committed to wakefulness, not watching over wholesome states, not devoted to developing the factors of enlightenment at the beginning and end of the night — then his body feels intoxicated, his eye does not see directions clearly, the Dhamma is not remembered by him. Sloth and torpor overcome his mind and remain. Without gladness, he lives the holy life. He has doubts about the true Dhamma. Therefore, monk, you should train thus: ‘I will guard the sense faculties, have moderation in eating, be committed to wakefulness, watch over wholesome states, and be devoted to developing the factors of enlightenment at the beginning and end of the night.’”

title: “Thus, monks, a clansman goes forth. He has desire for sensual pleasures, ardent craving, a mind of ill-will, defiled thoughts, lacking mindfulness, not clearly comprehending,…
content: “Thus, monks, a clansman goes forth. He has desire for sensual pleasures, ardent craving, a mind of ill-will, defiled thoughts, lacking mindfulness, not clearly comprehending, not concentrated, with distracted mind, with uncontrolled faculties. Monks, like a charnel-fire brand that is burning at both ends and smeared with feces in the middle, not used as fuel in the village nor in the forest — with that simile, I describe that person, who has lost both the householder’s enjoyment and the goal of the ascetic life.”

title: Elder Nun Sumedhā: “What is this foul, stinking body, Frightening, A leather bag full of corpses, Oozing impurities? What is this body I know —…
content:
Elder Nun Sumedhā:

“What is this foul, stinking body,
Frightening,
A leather bag full of corpses,
Oozing impurities?

What is this body I know —
Disgusting, smeared with flesh and blood,
A dwelling for worms,
Food for birds —
This body is like that —
To whom should I give it now?

The body, thrown in a charnel ground,
Not long, loses consciousness —
Like a discarded log —
Relatives are disgusted.

That body thrown in the charnel ground,
Becomes food for others —
Formerly they washed it clean,
Now they are disgusted —
Even parents are like that —
What to say of ordinary people?

They are infatuated with a body without core,
Bound by sinews and bones,
Full of saliva and tears,
Full of feces and urine, foul-smelling.

If this body were cut open,
Its inner parts revealed,
Even one’s mother would be disgusted,
Unable to bear the stench.

It is because of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases
That this body is constituted —
The root of renewed existence, suffering —
They speak of it rightly —
They do not delight in it at all.
So who would I wish to marry?

Even a hundred spears every day,
Constantly piercing the body —
Though harmed for a hundred years —
That would still be better,
Because that suffering,
In the end, would be destroyed.

The wise would agree to such killing,
As the Teacher declared —
They wander on for a long time,
With minds given to killing,
Continually following one after another.

In the realms of devas and humans,
Animals, asuras,
Hungry ghosts, and hell —
They undergo endless slaughter.

In hell, there are many —
Those with defiled minds, fallen —
The heavenly realm is no refuge —
There is no Nibbāna-like happiness there.

Those who attain Nibbāna
Are intimately connected
With the teaching
Of the One with Ten Powers —
At ease, unruffled,
Striving to end birth and death.

Today, father, I am determined to leave.
These empty possessions
Are of no value.
I am disgusted with sensual pleasures,
I am weary of sensual pleasures —
They have been cut off,
Like a palm tree stump.”

title: “Monks, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon your desire for it. And what, monks, is impermanent? Form, monks, is impermanent … Feeling … Perception ……
content: “Monks, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon your desire for it. And what, monks, is impermanent? Form, monks, is impermanent … Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Whatever is impermanent, monks, there you should abandon your desire.”

title: Elder Sivaka: Impermanent are these houses, Built again and again. Seeking the house-builder, Birth is suffering. O house-builder, you are seen! From now on, you…
content:
Elder Sivaka:

Impermanent are these houses,
Built again and again.
Seeking the house-builder,
Birth is suffering.

O house-builder, you are seen!
From now on, you cannot
Build a house again.
All your rafters are broken,
The ridge-pole is shattered.
The mind has been pushed from the stream,
Here, it is destroyed.

title: “Monks, when a monk has abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, then with the abandonment of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, he does…
content: “Monks, when a monk has abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, then with the abandonment of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, he does not form any volitional formation, does not generate any kamma. Without forming, without generating, he does not cling to anything in the world. Without clinging, he is not agitated. Without agitation, he personally attains Nibbāna. He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”

title: “Here, venerable sir, a person has a stain and he truly knows: ‘There is a stain in me.’ For such a person, it can be…
content: “Here, venerable sir, a person has a stain and he truly knows: ‘There is a stain in me.’ For such a person, it can be expected: ‘He will arouse desire, make effort, arouse energy to abandon that stain. He will die without greed, without ill-will, without delusion, without stain, his mind unpolluted.’ Venerable sir, just as a bronze bowl brought from the market or from the smithy, covered with dust and grime, and the owner uses it, wipes it, and does not throw it into a dusty place – that bowl, after a time, becomes more purified and cleaner.”

title: “Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — eaten by crows, or by hawks, or by vultures, or by dogs,…
content: “Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — eaten by crows, or by hawks, or by vultures, or by dogs, or by jackals, or by various worms. What do you think, monks? Has her former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Thus, monks, is the peril in the case of forms.”
